The Taklamakan Desert. A large hot desert in northwestern China, covering roughly one hundred thirty thousand square miles in the Xinjiang region between the Tian Shan and Kunlun mountain ranges. Its name, derived from Uyghur, traditionally meant go in and you will not come out, reflecting its extreme aridity, fierce winds, and historical danger to travelers. It is a critical section of the ancient Silk Road.

One of the world's largest sand deserts, the Taklamakan is the second-largest in the world after the Sahara. It is characterized by enormous dunes and complex sand patterns. Temperatures fluctuate wildly. Summers exceed forty-five degrees Celsius, or one hundred and thirteen degrees Fahrenheit, while winter nights can fall well below freezing. Annual rainfall is less than one inch in most areas.

The Taklamakan is surrounded by oasis cities—Kashgar, Samarkand, Bukhara—which served as vital nodes on the Silk Road's transcontinental trade network. Traversed by merchants, pilgrims, and armies for over two millennia, the Silk Road routes skirted its edges via oases, avoiding the interior.

The Taklamakan contains deposits of oil and natural gas. Modern drilling and exploration have increased economic interest and environmental impact. Uyghur and Tajik peoples have inhabited oasis settlements around its margins. The desert itself was largely unmapped and unexplored until the twentieth century.

Hazardous winds called black winds can obliterate visibility and landmarks, making navigation without modern technology extremely dangerous. The desert's status as a major obstacle and defining feature of the Silk Road trade route network underscores its historical importance. It occupies Chinese territory in the Xinjiang autonomous region, serving as the eastern anchor of Central Asian geography and culture, while Kashgar stands at its western edge as a major oasis city.
